narrative.h2: DJ visuals aren't music videos — they're festival projection, scaled down

sections.heading: Why the DJ MV is its own format
sections.body: DJs don't sing the song, didn't write the song the way a singer-songwriter did, and rarely appear on camera throughout. A DJ MV that tries to be a narrative artist video usually flops. What works is the festival-screen aesthetic shrunk down to YouTube: abstract motion graphics, mainstage-style visualizers, drop-synced light explosions, occasional cuts to the DJ behind the decks for identity. Think Anyma's visual sets, deadmau5's Cube projections, Eric Prydz's HOLO. Visual scale, not narrative depth.

sections.heading: What the drop has to look like
sections.body: Every DJ MV lives or dies on the drop. The 8 to 16 bars before it should build visually — color saturation creeping up, camera moves accelerating, framing tightening. The drop itself is the visual payoff: a hard cut to the widest, brightest, most kinetic shot in the video, sustained for the first 4 bars before any cuts return. Get that one moment right and the rest of the video can be loops; miss it and even great visuals feel flat under a great drop.

sections.heading: How Tunee builds the drop in
sections.body: The audio analyst flags the drop automatically (energy spike + tempo confirmation + structural cue), and Sage maps the visual buildup to land on it. The DJ preset skews toward abstract and architectural over character-driven — fewer faces, more geometry, palette locked to festival-screen brights. Output is 16:9 for venue playback files (yes, you can hand the MP4 to your VJ for live shows) plus 9:16 for social. Same generation, both surfaces.
